name: Inverse Genealogy
description: Ivan is fond of genealogy. Currently he is studying a particular genealogical structure, which consists of some people. In this structure every person has either both parents specified, or none. Additionally, each person has exactly one child, except for one special person, who does not have any children. The people in this structure are conveniently numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, and $$$s_i$$$ denotes the child of the person $$$i$$$ (and $$$s_i = 0$$$ for exactly one person who does not have any children). We say that $$$a$$$ is an ancestor of $$$b$$$ if either $$$a = b$$$, or $$$a$$$ has a child, who is an ancestor of $$$b$$$. That is $$$a$$$ is an ancestor for $$$a$$$, $$$s_a$$$, $$$s_{s_a}$$$, etc. We say that person $$$i$$$ is imbalanced in case this person has both parents specified, and the total number of ancestors of one of the parents is at least double the other. Ivan counted the number of imbalanced people in the structure, and got $$$k$$$ people in total. However, he is not sure whether he computed it correctly, and would like to check if there is at least one construction with $$$n$$$ people that have $$$k$$$ imbalanced people in total. Please help him to find one such construction, or determine if it does not exist.
input_specification: The input contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 100\,000$$$, $$$0 \leq k \leq n$$$), the total number of people and the number of imbalanced people.
output_specification: If there are no constructions with $$$n$$$ people and $$$k$$$ imbalanced people, output NO . Otherwise output YES on the first line, and then $$$n$$$ integers $$$s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n$$$ ($$$0 \leq s_i \leq n$$$), which describes the construction and specify the child of each node (or 0, if the person does not have any children).
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1379E — Inverse Genealogy [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
